title: Algebraic description of complex conjugation on cohomology of a smooth projective hypersurface

predicted_errors.error_location: Subsection 2.1, the displayed relative long exact sequence of the pair (P^n, P^n \ X) and the subsequent tubular-neighborhood isomorphism
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper writes '··· → H_{n-1}(P^n, P^n\X) → H_n(P^n\X) → H_n(P^n) → H_n(P^n, P^n\X) → ···' and then 'we have an isomorphism H_{n-1}(P^n, P^n\X) ≅ H_{n-1}(X)'. Both statements have the wrong index. In the long exact sequence of a pair the term mapping to H_n(P^n\X) is H_{n+1}(P^n, P^n\X), not H_{n-1}(P^n, P^n\X) (homological degree cannot increase along the sequence). Likewise the Thom/tubular-neighbourhood isomorphism for a complex codimension-one submanifold shifts degree by 2: H_{n+1}(P^n, P^n\X) ≅ H_{n-1}(X). Only with the corrected index does one obtain the tube map T: H_{n-1}(X) → H_n(P^n\X) that is subsequently used.

predicted_errors.error_location: Theorem 2.3 and its proof (end of Subsection 2.3), formula (2.10)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The theorem allows 'any polynomial y^{n-1-i} g_{j_i}(x) ∈ A_{c_X} such that f_{j_i}·g_{j_i} ∉ Jac(G)' and then defines the conjugate class as a scalar multiple of g_{j_i}. The proof says that finding the conjugate 'amounts to finding h_{j_i} such that R(y^i f_{j_i}, y^{n-1-i} h_{j_i}) = U_{k,γ}'. One linear condition does not determine a class in A_{c_X,(n-1-i)}/(Jac(S)∩A_{c_X,(n-1-i)}) whenever that space has dimension > 1: one would need the values R(U_l, h) for every basis element U_l of the complementary graded piece. Concretely, if h satisfies r_{f h} = 0 but [h] ≠ 0 (such h exists as soon as the graded piece has dimension > 1), then g and g+h give the same scalar in (2.10) but different classes f̃, both claimed to represent the same conjugate class — a contradiction. The theorem is therefore only valid when the relevant graded piece is one-dimensional (as in the elliptic-curve example).

Corollary 2.7 asserts (φ_C^{-1}∘P)(H^{n-1}_prim(X,R)) = Σ_j (R·[w_j] + R·[√−1 w_j]) with w_j = (y^i f_{j_i} + y^{n-1-i} f̃_{j_i})/2. Since w_j is by construction fixed by the (antilinear) conjugation, R·[w_j] + R·[√−1 w_j] = C·[w_j] is a complex line, and √−1 w_j is anti-invariant, hence NOT in the real cohomology. The right second generator is (y^i f_{j_i} − y^{n-1-i} f̃_{j_i})/(2√−1). Example 2.8 repeats the same mistake, writing R[(1+μ y D)/2] + √−1 R[(1+μ y D)/2], i.e. the full complex line C·[(1+μ y D)/2], which is not the (conjugation-fixed) real structure of H^1(X,R).

predicted_errors.error_location: Example 2.4 and Example 2.8 vs. Subsection 2.2 (definition of μ)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: In Subsection 2.2 μ is defined as the C-dimension of H^{n-1}_prim(X,C), and the stated formula gives μ = 2 for an elliptic curve (n=2, e=3). Example 2.4 then redefines 'μ := (∫_{γ_1}ω·∫_{γ_2}ω̄ − ∫_{γ_2}ω·∫_{γ_1}ω̄)/(24π√−1) ∈ C' and Example 2.8 uses this transcendental number as μ. The same symbol denotes two different, incompatible quantities (an integer dimension vs. a period ratio), making the examples contradict the earlier definition. (The symbol μ is also reused for a cohomology class in the proof of Lemma 2.5, 'for μ ∈ H^{2n-2}(X,C)'.)

predicted_errors.error_location: Example 2.4 ('the set {[1],[y u]} is a Q-basis of Q[y,x]/Jac(S)')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The quotient ring Q[y,x_0,x_1,x_2]/Jac(S) with Jac(S) = (yG_0, yG_1, yG_2, G) is infinite-dimensional (it contains Q[x]/(G) in y-degree 0), so a two-element set cannot be a Q-basis of it. The correct statement is that {[1],[y u]} is a basis of the charge-c_X graded piece A_{c_X}/(Jac(S) ∩ A_{c_X}), which is the space appearing in Theorem 2.1.

predicted_errors.error_location: Subsection 2.4 (odd n): definition of U_{k,γ} as a diagonal entry of P_X · P · P̄_X^T, and the claim that 'the same statement in Theorem 2.3 holds for n = 2m+1 by the same argument'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: For period vectors p = (∫_{γ_i}ω), q = (∫_{γ_j}η) relative to a basis {γ_i} of a homology lattice with intersection matrix P, one has ∫_X ω∧η = p^T (P^{-1})^T q. In the even-n case this coincides with the stated formula only because the symplectic lattice is unimodular (Q^{-1} = −Q, so (Q^{-1})^T = Q). In the odd-n case the paper itself notes det(γ_α·γ_β) = ±e ≠ ±1, so P ≠ (P^{-1})^T and the quantity Σ_{i,j} ∫_{γ_i}φ(U_k)(γ_i·γ_j)conj(∫_{γ_j}φ(U_k)) is not ∫_X φ(U_k)∧conj(φ(U_k)); the matrix P should be replaced by P^{-1}. Hence the proof of Theorem 2.3 does not carry over verbatim to odd n.
